chief_complaint: sudden severe prolonged fetal heart rate bradycardia immediately following artificial rupture of membranes
hpi_details: 28F G1P0 at 39 weeks experiencing abrupt fetal bradycardia down to 70 bpm after amniotomy where vaginal examination palpates a pulsating loop of umbilical cord protruding through the cervix requiring elevation of fetal presenting part and immediate STAT Cesarean delivery.
ideas: She thinks the baby got startled or tangled in something when her water broke.
concerns: She is terrified that her baby's heart will stop beating before they can deliver.
expectations: She hopes the medical team will rush her into an immediate emergency Cesarean to deliver the baby alive.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Umbilical cord prolapse evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Umbilical cord prolapse is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Cord Prolapse Acute Obstetric Emergency, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: An abrupt, persistent fetal bradycardia or recurrent variable decelerations immediately after membrane rupture should prompt immediate assessment for cord prolapse.
A pulsating umbilical cord palpated below the presenting part or seen at the introitus confirms overt umbilical cord prolapse.
This event commonly follows amniotomy when the presenting part is not well applied to the cervix; fetal hypoxia results from cord compression.
Diagnosis is clinical and must not be delayed for imaging: assess fetal heart rate continuously while preparing immediate delivery.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Umbilical cord prolapse.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Placental abruption without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fetal heart rate drop to 70 bpm.
management_principles: Call the obstetric emergency immediately and expedite cesarean delivery unless vaginal birth is clearly imminent and safer.
Relieve cord compression by manually elevating the presenting part and positioning the patient knee-chest or head-down lateral; bladder filling can be used if transfer is prolonged.
Avoid manipulating the cord; if it is exteriorized, cover it loosely with warm saline-soaked gauze and continue continuous fetal monitoring.
Do not delay delivery for further evaluation; consider tocolysis only when it does not delay definitive delivery and according to local protocol.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Cord Prolapse Acute Obstetric Emergency: sudden severe prolonged fetal heart rate bradycardia immediately following artificial rupture of membranes. 28F G1P0 at 39 weeks experiencing abrupt fetal bradycardia down to 70 bpm after amniotomy where vaginal examination palpates a pulsating loop of umbilical cord protruding through the cervix requiring elevation of fetal presenting part and immediate STAT Cesarean delivery.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Cord Prolapse Acute Obstetric Emergency.
reference_soap.assessment: Overt umbilical cord prolapse after amniotomy causing acute fetal bradycardia.
reference_soap.plan: Call the obstetric emergency and proceed to immediate cesarean delivery. Continuously elevate the presenting part manually; place the patient in knee-chest or steep head-down lateral position and consider bladder filling to relieve compression. Avoid handling the cord, keep it warm and moist if exteriorized, continue fetal monitoring, and do not delay delivery for further evaluation.

teaching.one_liner: 28F G1P0 at 39 weeks with sudden severe fetal bradycardia after amniotomy and a palpable pulsating cord on exam.
red_flags: Fetal heart rate drop to 70 bpm

must_ask.objective: Explain the emergency and next steps
must_ask.say: The umbilical cord has slipped down ahead of the baby — we need to move to an emergency C-section right now.

must_ask.objective: Instruct positioning to relieve cord compression
must_ask.say: I need you to get on your hands and knees right now to take pressure off the cord.

must_ask.objective: Reassure about manual elevation of presenting part
must_ask.say: I'm going to keep my hand in place to hold the baby's head off the cord until we reach the operating room.

must_ask.objective: Ask about time since rupture of membranes
must_ask.say: When exactly did your water break?

must_ask.objective: Reassure the patient amid the emergency
must_ask.say: I know this is frightening, but we are moving quickly to protect your baby.

history.answer: She was in active labor, but right after the doctor broke her water, the baby's heart monitor started blaring and dropped down to seventy.
She is at thirty-nine weeks today, right on schedule, and she has attended every one of her prenatal clinic visits.
It happened just five minutes ago right after they ruptured her amniotic sac; there was no injury, bump, or fall.
Her water was broken less than ten minutes ago, and the heart rate alarm went off almost immediately after.
A gush of clear fluid came out when they ruptured the membranes, and it looked normal without any bad odor or meconium.
She had only a small pinkish show on the pad, but no heavy bleeding or blood clots at all.
Her labor contractions come every three to four minutes, and her belly softens up completely between them without staying constantly rigid.
She felt the baby kicking actively earlier today until the membranes were ruptured just moments ago.
No, she has not had any severe headaches, blurry vision, or sudden swelling in her face or hands.
She has had no severe pain in the pit of her stomach or under her right ribs.
She is breathing fast because of fear, but she has not felt dizzy, lightheaded, or like passing out.
No, she has not had any fever, chills, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge.
Her routine ultrasounds showed a single normal-sized baby with the placenta located high and away from the cervix.
All her prenatal lab tests were normal, including her blood pressure, blood sugar challenge, and urine protein tests.
She gained around twelve kilograms steadily over the pregnancy and has had normal thirst and eating habits.
This is her first pregnancy, so she has never had a delivery, miscarriage, or termination before.
We will do whatever is needed right now; should she get onto her hands and knees with her chest down to take the pressure off?
Please do whatever protects the baby; if you have to keep your hand inside lifting the baby's head, please continue.
Is the umbilical cord slipping down, and does she need an immediate emergency C-section right now to deliver the baby?
Thank you for explaining quickly and keeping calm; we are terrified, but we understand this is an emergency.
I thought maybe the baby got tangled up or hurt when my water was broken.
Hearing the monitor drop so low makes me terrified that my baby's heart will give out.
Please rush me into an emergency C-section right away if that's what it takes to save my baby.
She has no chronic medical illnesses like hypertension, diabetes, asthma, or heart conditions.
She has never had any surgery or stayed in a hospital prior to this labor.
She has only taken standard prenatal vitamins and iron supplements throughout pregnancy.
She has no known allergies to any antibiotics, pain medications, or latex.
She has never smoked cigarettes, used e-cigarettes, or taken any recreational drugs.
She has completely abstained from alcohol before and during the entire pregnancy.
She works in an office as an accountant and lives at home with me.
Her family has no history of birth defects, early infant loss, or bleeding problems.
Her last menstrual period was thirty-nine weeks ago, and her periods were always regular twenty-eight-day cycles.

exam.finding: The patient is visibly anxious and in active labor, lying supine with fetal monitor alarms sounding.
Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C.
Gravid abdomen with fundal height consistent with term pregnancy; uterus relaxes fully and remains non-tender between regular contractions.
Doppler auscultation reveals persistent, profound fetal bradycardia at 70 beats per minute.
Digital vaginal examination confirms an overt, pulsating loop of umbilical cord palpated below the fetal presenting part protruding through the cervix.
Trace physiologic dependent pretibial edema bilaterally without pitting or calf tenderness.
Patellar deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally with normal relaxation and no clonus.
